bessemer-process-1856.verification_note: Britannica confirms development and patenting in 1856, and the primary patent confirms the air-injection method. Neither source confirms an announcement; the patent is dated November 11, 1856.
bessemer-process-1856.detail: His first licensees produced poor steel, "rotten hot and rotten cold" in a friend's words, because impurities in their iron were not burned off cleanly. Metallurgist Robert Forester Mushet solved this by burning off all carbon, then adding spiegeleisen, an iron and manganese alloy, in exact amounts. American William Kelly claimed to have found a similar process independently in 1851, a dispute still unsettled. Using Bessemer's process, Carnegie Steel cut rail prices from $100 to $50 per ton between 1873 and 1875.

bombay-cotton-mill-davar-1856.summary: Parsi merchant Cowasji Nanabhoy Davar floated Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company in 1854 and began spinning in February 1856 at Tardeo with machinery from Lancashire and a steam engine. Indian capital, Indian management and local cotton from Gujarat and Deccan distinguished it from Calcutta's Scottish-run jute mills. By 1875 Bombay had 27 mills and by 1900 over 80, selling coarse yarn to China and cloth to inland India. Mill labour drawn from Konkan and Deccan villages built chawl neighbourhoods of Girangaon. This industry financed Tata and other houses and created an industrial working class whose strikes shaped Indian politics.

Chandavarkar's Cambridge monograph examines workers, neighbourhoods and business strategy in Bombay cotton industry between 1900 and 1940. mendel-pea-genetics-1856.summary: In 1856 Gregor Mendel, Augustinian friar in Brno, began crossing pea varieties and, over eight years and some 28,000 plants, found rules of inheritance that nobody took up until 1900. Abbot Cyril Napp had permitted him to plan a hybridization programme in 1854, and from 1854 to 1856 he tested 34 varieties for constancy of their traits before making crosses (Britannica, Robert Olby). He chose seven traits expressed distinctly, such as tall or short plants and green or yellow seeds, and crossed true-breeding lines. Ratios in his second generation led him to his laws of segregation and independent assortment; he read his results to Brno's Natural History Society in February and March 1865 and published Versuche über Pflanzen-Hybriden in 1866. Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak independently confirmed his findings in 1900, and genetics began.

mendel-pea-genetics-1856.detail: In his second generation one plant in four showed its recessive trait, two were hybrids and one bred true for its dominant trait; Mendel coined dominant and recessive to explain how green seeds could vanish in one generation and return in another.

perkin-mauveine-1856.summary: In 1856 an 18-year-old William Perkin made a purple dye from coal tar by accident, founding the synthetic chemicals industry. He oxidised aniline with potassium dichromate; toluidine impurities reacted with it and left black solid, apparent failure, but when he cleaned his flask with alcohol he noticed purple portions in solution. Mauveine launched synthetic dyemaking as an industry, and newer synthetic colours had displaced it by 1870.

perkin-mauveine-1856.detail: It dyed silk and other textiles, so Perkin patented it and in 1857 opened his dyeworks at Greenford, beside Middlesex's Grand Union Canal, to mass-produce it. First called aniline purple, it was named mauve in England in 1859 after French for mallow; between 1859 and 1861 mauve became a fashion must-have.

victoria-eight-hour-day-1856.summary: In April 1856 Melbourne stonemasons marched from their site to Parliament and won an eight-hour day, among the first workers anywhere to do so and without loss of pay; Sydney stonemasons had won it earlier. In Melbourne, negotiations with employers and government produced agreement that stonemasons would work eight hours for their old ten-hour wage, and public works labourers would get eight hours with no loss of pay. By 1858 eight-hour working was firmly established in Victoria's building industry, and from 1879 Victoria marked it with a public holiday.

victoria-eight-hour-day-1856.detail: Many were skilled tradesmen drawn by Victoria's gold rush, some veteran Chartists from Britain. Stephens recalled that "it was a burning hot day and I thought the occasion a good one". Sydney's stonemasons had won eight hours earlier, in 1855 by Scalmer's account or March 1856 by others, at reduced wages. Stonemasons and other trades celebrated with a holiday and procession on 12 May 1856.

victoria-secret-ballot-1856.summary: In 1856 Victoria introduced the secret ballot, history's first mandatorily secret, government-printed ballot; this Australian ballot spread worldwide. Before this, Australian colonies followed English practice and voted on the voices, each elector calling out his candidates' names in public, which left him open to bribery and intimidation. In secret voting each elector marks his paper ballot without revealing it and places it in a sealed box, so no one can tell how anyone voted.

sources.author: Brent, Peter

victoria-secret-ballot-1856.verification_note: Brent (2006, 2023) calls Victoria's 1856 law history's first mandatorily secret, government-printed ballot; Tasmania and South Australia legislated in those same months, so Victoria was not alone in voting in private by law.
victoria-secret-ballot-1856.detail: Former Melbourne mayor William Nicholson pioneered Victoria's law; Tasmania's act of 7 February 1856 came earlier, rediscovered only recently, and South Australia legislated in those same months. In America, where partisan newspapers printed filled-out ballots for party workers to hand out, Massachusetts adopted its state-wide version in 1888, and Americans still call secret ballots Australian ballots.

western-union-formed-1856.summary: In 1856 two telegraph companies merged as Western Union; within five years it wired North America and held a near monopoly. It completed America's first transcontinental telegraph in 1861, with its first messages going to President Abraham Lincoln, and in 1866 bought both remaining rivals, American Telegraph Company and United States Telegraph Company, gaining for a time a virtual monopoly over American telegraphy.

Selden, Hiram Sibley and others had founded it in Rochester, New York, in 1851; Cornell, John James Speed and Francis Ormand Jonathan Smith controlled Erie and Michigan. In 1857 Western Union joined six of America's largest telegraph firms in their Treaty of Six Nations, carving regional monopolies with shared main lines, then kept buying rivals large and small until by 1864 only two serious competitors remained.

atlantic-cable-celebration-1858.summary: In August 1858 New York celebrated history's first telegraph message across the Atlantic with fireworks. That cable, laid by Cyrus Field's Atlantic Telegraph Company between Ireland and Newfoundland, had carried its first message on 16 August: "Europe and America are united by telegraphy. Glory to God in the highest; on earth, peace and good will towards men." Within weeks senior engineer Wildman Whitehouse, who believed higher voltage was needed, had ruined its insulation, and it was inoperable by early September.

Then Queen Victoria and President James Buchanan exchanged congratulations; her 98-word message took 16 hours to send because signals were hard to decipher. Buchanan called it "a triumph more glorious, because far more useful to mankind, than was ever won by conqueror on the field of battle".

great-stink-sewers-1858.summary: In 1858 sewage stench in the Thames drove Parliament to fund London's sewers. On 15 June Disraeli tabled a bill calling the Thames "a Stygian pool, reeking with ineffable and intolerable horrors"; it made London's Metropolitan Board of Works responsible for cleaning up and let it borrow £3 million, repaid through three pence levied on London households over forty years. Sewage no longer reached Thames shores, cholera outbreaks ended, and engineer Bazalgette is thought to have saved more lives than any other Victorian official.

great-stink-sewers-1858.verification_note: A book abstract confirms this 1858 sewage-stench context, but does not establish sewer reforms, funding details or claimed health outcomes. Parliament's page had no readable text.
great-stink-sewers-1858.detail: Victorian doctors mostly held miasma theory, that disease spread through contaminated air, so officials had flushed London's sewers regularly, sending still more sewage into its river. Three cholera outbreaks had already been blamed on it. By June that stench so disrupted Parliament, beside the river, that curtains on its river side were soaked in lime chloride, and Chancellor Benjamin Disraeli was seen leaving a committee room with his handkerchief to his nose. Chief engineer Joseph Bazalgette planned to carry sewage eastward: 1,100 miles of street sewers feeding 82 miles of main interconnecting sewers, with pumping stations lifting waste to higher pipes. Construction began in 1859 and lasted until 1875.

picture.credit: Punch Magazine, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

lenoir-engine-1858.summary: In 1858 Lenoir built the first working internal combustion engine, burning gas inside the cylinder; in 1863 his Hippomobile carriage ran on one. His engine was a steam engine converted to burn coal gas mixed with air, ignited by "jumping sparks" from a Ruhmkorff coil, with power strokes at each end of its cylinder; its mixture was not compressed before ignition, so it ran quietly but inefficiently. Other engineers, especially Nicolaus Otto, soon improved on his design and made it obsolete.

lenoir-engine-1858.detail: He unveiled it to twenty guests on 23 January 1860, turned on the gas valve, pushed the flywheel, and it came to life. Backed by two million francs, his Société des Moteurs Lenoir built engines in Rue de la Roquette; by 1865, 143 had been sold in Paris alone and Reading Gas Works in London had begun production. In 1863 his Hippomobile, a carriage with such an engine, drove 18 km from Paris to Joinville-le-Pont in three hours.

transatlantic-cable-1858-1858.summary: In August 1858 the first telegraph message crossed the Atlantic by cable; in September, after several days of deterioration, it failed altogether. Chief electrician Wildman Whitehouse, a medical doctor self-taught in electrical engineering, had long disputed physicist William Thomson's law of squares, which predicted slow signalling on long cables; at Valentia Whitehouse connected his own equipment and drove up to 2,000 volts through it to get faster operation. That, with poor handling and design, compromised its insulation. Some writers hinted it had been a hoax.

transatlantic-cable-1858-1858.detail: Thomson had read clear signals throughout the laying voyage with his sensitive mirror galvanometer. Whitehouse could not read Queen Victoria's confirmation copy for days, took it from Thomson's galvanometer and re-entered it in his printing telegraph to pretend otherwise. Whitehouse was held responsible and dismissed. A durable connection, laid from Brunel's SS Great Eastern, entered service on 27 July 1866, and both continents have been cabled together ever since.

darwin-origin-of-species-1859.summary: In November 1859 Darwin published On the Origin of Species, arguing all species descend from common ancestors. Written for non-specialist readers at fifteen shillings, it drew on his Beagle voyage of the 1830s and twenty years of research and experiment. Within two decades scientists widely agreed that evolution with branching common descent had occurred, though they were slow to grant natural selection as much weight as Darwin gave it.

darwin-origin-of-species-1859.detail: Booksellers had taken every copy of its 1,250-copy first printing at John Murray's sale two days earlier. Reading Thomas Malthus in 1838, Darwin had related human populations' struggle to survive to wildlife, seeing that well-adapted variations would be passed on while unfavourable ones were destroyed. He published only after Alfred Russel Wallace sent him a paper reaching similar conclusions in June 1858; friends arranged a joint reading at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858. Most naturalists then held species to be unchanging parts of a designed hierarchy.

picture.alt: Title page of Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species, first edition of 1859.
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public domain, via Wellcome Collection

drake-oil-well-1859.summary: In 1859 Edwin Drake struck oil near Titusville, Pennsylvania, in what Britannica calls America's first productive oil well. Seneca Oil Company had put Drake in charge in 1858, and northwestern Pennsylvania boomtowns followed his 69-foot strike. Drilling had reached oil earlier: at Bibi-Heybat near Baku, reported in 1848, while James Miller Williams was refining Ontario petroleum by 1857, though whether his early wells were drilled or dug is unknown. Producing 12 to 20 barrels daily as prices plummeted, Drake's well never made a profit and stopped in 1861.

sources.title: Drake Well - Wikipedia
sources.confirms: Background only: Seneca Oil Company organized in March 1858 'to place Drake in charge of producing petroleum'; 'The well produced 12 to 20 barrels (2 to 3 m3) a day, but, after the price of oil plummeted from the resulting boom, it was never profitable'; 'The well stopped producing in 1861'.

sources.title: Britannica, "Edwin Drake | American Oil Pioneer & Father of the Oil Industry"
sources.confirms: 'the driller of the first productive oil well in the United States'; Seneca Oil Company formed by New Haven stockholders who 'sent him back to develop the site'; 'He began drilling in May 1858'; oil reached 'at a depth of 69 feet (21 metres) on August 27, 1859'; 'With the spread of Drake's drilling techniques, Titusville and other northwestern Pennsylvania communities became boomtowns.'
sources.qualifies: The article describes the well as the first productive oil well in the United States, but does not call it the first commercial oil well.
sources.author: Britannica Editors

sources.title: Pratt, J. A., review of Brian Frehner, Finding Oil: The Nature of Petroleum Geology, 1859-1920 (University of Nebraska Press, 2011), Journal of American History 99 (2012)
sources.author: Pratt, J. A.

sources.author: Hennadii Haiko, Volodymyr Biletsky

Vorontsov informed that the first well which found oil was drilled in Bibi-Heybat. Unfortunately, as in the case with Romania oil well in 1821, the oil deposit was limited and did not gain further industrial meaning'; 'A new wave of interest in well's extraction technologies appeared in 1860-s after successful experience of well's drilling in Galichina (beginning from 1854) and especially in Pennsylvania (from 1859).'

sources.venue: Dictionary of Canadian Biography, vol. 11, University of Toronto/Universite Laval
sources.author: Norman R. Ball, Edward Phelps
sources.confirms: 'By 1857 J. M. Williams and Company was refining petroleum, albeit crudely, at Oil Springs, Lambton County, and by 1860 Williams had set up a refinery in Hamilton'; 'Much fruitless debate has taken place over whether Williams was the first man in North America to drill successfully for oil. A claim has been made for Edwin Laurentine Drake of Pennsylvania. Williams was working finds before Drake, but because he left no record of his work, and his early ventures were of little interest to contemporary journalists, there is no way of knowing whether his early wells were drilled or dug and cribbed. The significant fact is that he was the first entrepreneur with sufficient capital, business acumen, technical understanding, and tenacity to tackle the petroleum of Lambton County.'

sources.venue: University of California, San Diego, working paper dated December 22, 2010, revised February 1, 2011 (NBER Working Paper 16790), p. 2

sources.author: Ernest C. Miller
sources.confirms: 'This question comes about because in recent years some Canadian oil men have claimed that the first well in North America was drilled by James Miller Williams, at Enniskillen (later known as Oil Springs), Ontario, prior to the Drake Well which came in August 27, 1859.'
sources.qualifies: Miller argues Drake's priority against Williams; cited for the dispute's existence and Drake's August 27, 1859 date, not for its verdict.

drake-oil-well-1859.verification_note: Britannica confirms Drake's 1859 strike as America's first productive oil well, without calling it first commercial well or giving production figures or boom details; its journal source is cited as supporting literature. Summary replaced after a historian's read: Drake's was not the first well drilled for oil. Skhid (2019) records a Bibi-Heybat well near Baku whose oil find Viceroy Vorontsov reported in July 1848; the Dictionary of Canadian Biography records James Miller Williams working Ontario finds before Drake and states whether his early wells were drilled or dug cannot be known. Britannica's phrase 'first productive oil well in the United States' is kept as its own attribution, and its boomtowns line carries the boom; Hamilton dates a new era to Drake's 69-foot well. The Dictionary of Canadian Biography has Williams refining petroleum at Oil Springs by 1857. Production of 12 to 20 barrels a day, no profit and the 1861 stop sit on Wikipedia only; no opened independent page carries them.
drake-oil-well-1859.detail: Petroleum seeps along Oil Creek had been known to Native Americans for centuries. In 1855 George Bissell and Jonathan Eveleth, Seneca Oil's founders, had Yale chemist Benjamin Silliman test a sample, and his report described how to distil it into kerosene. Earlier American wells were drilled for salt brine and gave oil only as accidental byproduct; Drake decided to drill as salt wells were drilled rather than dig, hired Smith, a blacksmith and salt-well driller, drove through 32 feet of soil with a 6-horsepower steam engine, and sank 50 feet of cast iron pipe to stop groundwater collapsing his hole. His backers gave up in April 1859, so he borrowed $500 to continue.

pony-express-1860.summary: In 1860 the Pony Express carried mail across the West in ten days by relays of riders; telegraphy bankrupted it in 18 months. Its first riders left St. Joseph, Missouri and Sacramento on 3 April 1860 and each arrived 10 days later. Despite a heavy subsidy it never paid; it announced its closure on 26 October 1861, two days after America's transcontinental telegraph reached Salt Lake City and joined Omaha to Sacramento.

sources.title: Pony Express - Wikipedia
Britannica, "Pony Express | U.S. Mail Delivery, History, & Map"
sources.confirms: The page dates the Pony Express from April 1860 to October 1861 and says it ceased with completion of the transcontinental telegraph system.
sources.qualifies: It gives no exact closure day or date for completion of the telegraph.

sources.title: Cottrell, Wayne D., "On the History of the Pony Express and Extending Its Operation into the Telegraph Era," Transportation Research Record 2238 (2011)
sources.author: Cottrell, Wayne D.
sources.confirms: Abstract read via index record: the Pony Express operated from April 1860 until October 1861, covered the route in no more than 10 days, and ceased amid huge financial losses and completion of the transcontinental telegraph.
sources.qualifies: The abstract frames the cessation as amid both financial losses and telegraph completion, rather than stating that the telegraph alone bankrupted the service.

sources.title: Carey, Arthur C., "Effects of the Pony Express and the Transcontinental Telegraph upon Selected California Newspapers," Journalism Quarterly 51 (1974)
sources.author: Carey, Arthur C.
sources.confirms: Bibliographic record confirms a 1974 article on the effects of the Pony Express and transcontinental telegraph on selected California newspapers; text not read.

pony-express-1860.verification_note: Britannica and a journal abstract confirm an April 1860 to October 1861 operating period and its connection to telegraph completion; exact departure and arrival dates, October 26 closure and a two-day interval rest on other accounts.
pony-express-1860.detail: Gold had drawn thousands to California after 1848, and by 1860 its population was 380,000. Freight partners Russell, Majors and Waddell organised it in two months, with riders changing to fresh horses at swing stations 5 to 25 miles apart. It had shown that a year-round transcontinental communications system could work, and once replaced it soon became Old West lore.

picture.alt: Engraving of a Pony Express rider at full gallop, from an 1880 book on Colorado.
picture.credit: British Library, Public domain, via Europeana

self-strengthening-movement-1861.summary: From 1861 Qing China's Self-Strengthening Movement introduced Western methods and technology to renovate military, diplomatic, fiscal and educational policy, until defeat by Japan in 1895 ended it. Scholar Feng Guifen, its ideological champion, urged China to use barbarians' superior techniques to control barbarians; Prince Gong supported it in Beijing and headed China's new Zongli Yamen, in effect its foreign ministry. Western military training seen during cooperation against Taiping rebels stimulated it. Regional leaders who had raised Western-armed militias ran its ventures: Zeng Guofan's Shanghai arsenal, Li Hongzhang's arsenals at Nanjing and Tianjin, Zuo Zongtang's Fuzhou dockyard, language schools from 1862. Britannica notes that after 1885 lower officials and comprador intellectuals pressed for institutional reform and a parliament; Kwang-Ching Liu (Cambridge History of China, 1978) frames these years as dynastic restoration facing foreign peoples whose material culture surpassed China's own.

sources.title: Self-Strengthening Movement - Wikipedia
Britannica, "Self-Strengthening Movement"
sources.confirms: The article dates the movement to 1861-95 and describes Qing efforts to use Western methods and technology.
sources.qualifies: The article says the movement sought to renovate military, diplomatic, fiscal, and educational policy, a broader scope than the record's claim that China changed nothing else.

sources.title: Liu, Kwang-Ching, "The Ch'ing Restoration" (Cambridge University Press, 1978)
sources.author: Liu, Kwang-Ching
sources.confirms: Abstract read via index record: the chapter discusses Qing restoration after the Taiping rebellion and the survival of imperial authority; it does not verify the movement's named 1861 actions or its ending after the 1895 defeat.

self-strengthening-movement-1861.verification_note: Corrected in November 2026: its claim that China changed nothing beyond buying arms is dropped after Britannica, which describes reforms across military, diplomatic, fiscal and educational policy, and Liu (Cambridge History of China, 1978), who frames these years as restoration.
self-strengthening-movement-1861.detail: Beijing's Tongwen Guan, opened in 1862, trained diplomats and pioneered Western studies, and Jiangnan Arsenal translated 143 Western books between 1868 and 1879. Through 1870s and 1880s successors added shipping, telegraph lines and railways, often with foreign advisers.

picture.alt: Studio portrait photograph of Li Hongzhang, Qing official who led Self-Strengthening industrial projects.
picture.credit: Rijksmuseum, Public domain, via Europeana

cinchona-plantations-nilgiris-1862.summary: After Clements Markham smuggled cinchona seedlings out of Andes in 1860, Madras government planted them at Ootacamund in Nilgiri hills and Bengal government at Mungpoo near Darjeeling, with first commercial bark harvests from 1862. William McIvor at Ootacamund devised mossing, wrapping stripped trunks so bark regrew richer in alkaloids. Government factories at Mungpoo made cheap quinine and later cinchona febrifuge, sold through post offices at a few pice a dose from 1890s. Indian malaria control, army health and plantation labour all depended on this supply. Later Dutch Java plantations with higher yielding Cinchona ledgeriana dominated world market.

sources.title: Rohan Deb Roy, Malarial Subjects: Empire, Medicine and Nonhumans in British India, 1820-1909 (Cambridge University Press, 2017)
sources.author: Rohan Deb Roy
sources.confirms: cinchona plantations, quinine factories, post office sales

sources.title: Wellcome Collection, 'Cinchona plantations in India', archival materials
sources.confirms: plantation records and photographs

cinchona-plantations-nilgiris-1862.verification_note: Deb Roy monograph confirmed through open access publisher record; details follow its chapters as summarised in reviews.
cinchona-plantations-nilgiris-1862.detail: Deb Roy's Malarial Subjects (Cambridge, 2017) analyses cinchona cultivation, quinine manufacture and distribution in British India as a project tied to governance and markets. Harvest dates vary by source: planting 1860 to 1861, bark sales from 1862 onwards.

picture.alt: Engraving of cinchona plantations in the Nilgiri hills, Illustrated London News, 1862
picture.credit: The ILLUSTRATED LONDON NEWS

marshall-islands-stick-charts-1862.summary: Marshallese navigators tied sticks and shells into charts of ocean swells, a way of mapping the sea that Europeans first recorded in 1862. Navigators crouched or lay prone in their canoes to feel how underlying swells pitched and rolled them, sensing each island's "shadow" in bent and crossing swells; charts were studied and memorised before a voyage and left ashore at sea. In 1862 missionary L.H. Gulick described them for Western readers in Nautical Magazine, its first public notice; no date is known for when they were invented.

sources.title: Marshall Islands stick chart - Wikipedia
How Sticks and Shell Charts Became a Sophisticated System for Navigation - Smithsonian

Genz, Joseph; Aucan, Jerome; Merrifield, Mark; Finney, Ben; Joel, Korent; Kelen, Alson, 'Wave Navigation in the Marshall Islands: Comparing Indigenous and Western Scientific Knowledge of the Ocean', Oceanography 22, no. 2 (2009)
sources.author: Genz, Joseph; Aucan, Jerome; Merrifield, Mark; Finney, Ben; Joel, Korent; Kelen, Alson
sources.confirms: The article confirms that Marshallese navigators remotely sense land from how islands disrupt swells and documents the wave concepts behind the stick charts through fieldwork with surviving navigators.

sources.title: Playdon, George W., 'The Significance of Marshallese Stick Charts', Journal of Navigation 20, no. 2 (1967)
sources.author: Playdon, George W.
sources.confirms: The abstract states some 20 to 30 charts survive in museums and examines their authenticity and meaning as swell diagrams; Crossref record confirmed.

marshall-islands-stick-charts-1862.verification_note: Genz et al. (2009) and Playdon (1967) confirm these charts as swell maps memorised before voyages; Gulick's 1862 notice in Nautical Magazine is their conventional first Western description, and their invention date is unknown.
marshall-islands-stick-charts-1862.detail: Only select rulers knew how to make them, passing it from father to son, so fifteen or more canoes sailed together behind a pilot. German naval captain Winkler described the system comprehensively in 1898. Stick charts remain cartography's only known system for mapping ocean swells; their use ended after the Second World War.

picture.alt: Marshallese rebbelib stick chart of palm ribs and shells mapping swell patterns, photographed in the 1920s.
picture.credit: Library of Congress Geography and Map Division, No known copyright restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons

pasteur-germ-theory-1862.summary: In 1862 France's Academy of Sciences awarded Pasteur its Alhumbert Prize of 2,500 francs for sealed-flask experiments showing that microbes in liquids come from dust in air. Spontaneous generation, belief that life arises from non-living matter, still had defenders; Félix Pouchet, director of Rouen's natural history museum, held that air anywhere could generate organisms in liquids and sternly criticised Pasteur's fermentation findings. The Academy had offered its prize to whoever could prove that doctrine true or false.

sources.title: Louis Pasteur - Wikipedia
Britannica, "Louis Pasteur | Biography, Inventions, Achievements, Germ Theory, & Facts"
sources.confirms: The article says Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation and contributed to germ theory, but does not give the date or details of the flask experiments or prize.

sources.title: Roll-Hansen, Nils, "Revisiting the Pouchet-Pasteur controversy over spontaneous generation: understanding experimental method," History and Philosophy of the Life Sciences 40 (2018)
sources.author: Roll-Hansen, Nils
sources.venue: History and Philosophy of the Life Sciences
sources.confirms: The abstract describes Pasteur's defeat of belief in spontaneous generation and says the controversy centered on the outcomes and conduct of experiments.

sources.title: Roll-Hansen, Nils, "Experimental Method and Spontaneous Generation: The Controversy between Pasteur and Pouchet, 1859-64," Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences 34 (1979), pp. 273-292
sources.author: Roll-Hansen, Nils
sources.venue: Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences
sources.confirms: The bibliographic record identifies a scholarly article about the Pasteur-Pouchet controversy from 1859 to 1864; the abstract text provided is incomplete.

pasteur-germ-theory-1862.verification_note: Britannica and journal sources support Pasteur's challenge to spontaneous generation and a broader Pasteur-Pouchet controversy; his 1862 flask date and Alhumbert Prize rest on other accounts.
pasteur-germ-theory-1862.detail: Pasteur boiled liquid in flasks and let only hot air in; nothing grew. He opened flasks of boiled liquid to dust and organisms grew, fewer at high altitude where air carried less dust. In swan-neck flasks, where air entered through a long curving tube that trapped dust, broth stayed clear unless tilted to touch its neck's contaminated walls. Organisms came from outside, on dust, not from within liquids or from pure air.

picture.alt: Swan-necked glass flask used by Louis Pasteur in his experiments against spontaneous generation.
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0, via Wellcome Collection

butler-darwin-among-machines-1863.summary: In 1863 Samuel Butler argued in print that machines evolve and may one day supplant us, history's first such warning. His letter, signed Cellarius, appeared in The Press in Christchurch as Darwin Among the Machines. It suggested machines might be "mechanical life" undergoing constant evolution and might eventually supplant humans as dominant species. Butler developed this and later articles into The Book of the Machines, three chapters of his novel Erewhon, published anonymously in 1872, whose society had long ago destroyed most mechanical inventions in an uprising.

sources.title: Darwin among the Machines - Wikipedia
'Darwin Among the Machines,' The Press (Christchurch, 13 June 1863)
sources.author: Cellarius
sources.confirms: The page identifies the article as appearing in The Press, Christchurch, on 13 June 1863, and shows it signed "Cellarius."

sources.title: Breuer, Hans-Peter, 'Samuel Butler's "The Book of the Machines" and the Argument from Design', Modern Philology 72 (1975), 365-383
sources.author: Breuer, Hans-Peter
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed study of the Book of the Machines chapters of Erewhon and their roots in Butler's New Zealand writing; the publisher page confirms the bibliographic data.

butler-darwin-among-machines-1863.verification_note: A digitized article confirms newspaper, place, date and Cellarius signature. It does not explicitly identify Samuel Butler as its author or establish its primacy claim.
butler-darwin-among-machines-1863.detail: Reviewers took those chapters as mocking Darwin; Butler protested he meant no mockery and wrote to Darwin saying his target was Joseph Butler's 1736 Analogy of Religion. Philosopher Louis Flaccus called it "a mixture of fun, satire, and thoughtful speculation". In 1998 George Dyson applied Butler's premise to Alan Turing's artificial life and intelligence in his own Darwin Among the Machines.

picture.alt: Photograph of Samuel Butler in 1858, a year before he sailed for New Zealand.
picture.credit: Published by Dutton, NY, 1920, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

london-underground-1863.summary: In 1863 London opened the first underground railway, gas-lit wooden carriages hauled by steam locomotives between Paddington and Farringdon. London's mainline termini stopped at its edge while up to 200,000 people entered the City on foot each day, and carts, cabs and omnibuses jammed its roads; City solicitor Charles Pearson had promoted railway schemes since 1846, and Parliament approved this one on 7 August 1854.

sources.title: Metropolitan Railway
Britannica, "London Underground | History, Routes, & Facts"
sources.confirms: Britannica states that the line opened on January 10, 1863, between Farringdon Street and Bishop's Road, Paddington, using steam locomotives.
sources.qualifies: The page does not explicitly identify the line as the first underground railway and gives fuller endpoint names.

sources.title: "Metropolitan Underground Railway, London," Scientific American
sources.confirms: Bibliographic record confirms a Scientific American item titled "Metropolitan Underground Railway, London" dated 1877; text not read.

london-underground-1863.verification_note: Britannica confirms its opening date, route and steam locomotives; a Scientific American item is cited as supporting literature, and its primacy claim rests on general histories.
london-underground-1863.detail: Money came slowly until 1858, when Pearson arranged for the City to buy £200,000 of shares. Navvies dug it mostly by cut-and-cover, trenching along New Road and roofing it over, then in tunnel and cutting beside Farringdon Road and culverted River Fleet; it was complete by late 1862 at £1.3 million. Pearson died that September. On opening day it carried 38,000 passengers.

picture.alt: Engraving of Metropolitan Railway's Baker Street station platforms around 1863, lit by gas and daylight shafts.
picture.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

pasteurization-1864.summary: In 1864 Pasteur showed that briefly heating wine killed microbes souring it; his method now keeps milk safe worldwide. It could then be aged without souring or losing quality. Local aged wines often turned acidic; his method was gentler than Nicolas Appert's bottling and boiling of 1810. Later named pasteurization, it was first used for wine and beer; Franz von Soxhlet proposed applying it to milk in 1886.

sources.title: Pasteurization (Wikipedia)
Britannica, "Pasteurization | Definition, Process, Inventor, & Facts"
sources.confirms: Britannica says Pasteur demonstrated in the 1860s that heating wine and beer could prevent abnormal fermentation.
sources.qualifies: The source dates the demonstration to "the 1860s," not specifically to 1864.

sources.title: Pasteur, Louis, Études sur le vin, ses maladies, causes qui les provoquent, procédés nouveaux pour le conserver et pour le vieillir (Imprimerie impériale, 1866)
sources.author: Pasteur, Louis
sources.confirms: The archive catalogue confirms a 1866 publication of Pasteur's book on wine diseases and methods for preserving and aging wine; the text was not read.
sources.qualifies: The catalogue dates the book to 1866, but does not establish that Pasteur developed the heat treatment in 1864.

pasteurization-1864.verification_note: Britannica confirms heat treatment of wine and beer in 1860s without giving 1864; Pasteur's 1866 Études sur le vin, his own publication of his heating method, is cited as supporting literature.
pasteurization-1864.detail: Bacteria soon proliferate in milk kept at room temperature, and tuberculosis caught from milk killed some 65,000 people in England and Wales between 1912 and 1937 alone. Mandatory milk pasteurization laws came much later, with a first US state law in 1947 and a federal requirement for interstate milk in 1973.

picture.alt: Wood engraving of Louis Pasteur at a microscope in his laboratory, published in 1885.
picture.credit: Adrien Marie, Public domain, via Wellcome Collection

red-cross-geneva-1864.summary: In August 1864 twelve states signed the first Geneva Convention, protecting wounded soldiers and those who tend them; no codified international treaty had covered battlefield sick and wounded before. Geneva businessman Henry Dunant had visited wounded men after Solferino in 1859 and was shocked to find 40,000 left on that field for want of facilities, personnel and truces; his 1862 book A Memory of Solferino proposed a permanent relief agency for wartime aid and a treaty recognising its neutrality.

sources.title: red-cross-geneva
Britannica, "Geneva Conventions"
sources.confirms: The article states that Henri Dunant initiated the negotiations that produced the Convention for the Amelioration of the Wounded in Time of War in 1864.
sources.qualifies: The page does not mention the August signing, the number of signatory states, or the events at Solferino.

sources.title: Convention for the Amelioration of the Condition of the Wounded in Armies in the Field. Geneva, 22 August 1864
sources.venue: International Committee of the Red Cross website
sources.confirms: The treaty record dates the convention's adoption to 22 August 1864 and describes protections for wounded people and neutrality for medical personnel and facilities.
sources.qualifies: The page reports that 16 states were represented at the conference, but does not state how many signed the Convention.

red-cross-geneva-1864.verification_note: ICRC's treaty record confirms adoption on 22 August 1864 and protections for wounded men and medical services, and Britannica confirms Dunant's role in initiating negotiations; ICRC reports 16 states represented, so twelve signatories rests on other accounts.
red-cross-geneva-1864.detail: In 1863 he co-founded International Committee of the Red Cross with lawyer Gustave Moynier. Switzerland invited every European government plus the United States, Brazil and Mexico to Geneva; 16 countries sent 26 delegates, presided over by General Guillaume Henri Dufour. Dunant shared 1901's first Nobel Peace Prize, and revised conventions followed in 1906 and 1949.

hsbc-founded-1865.summary: In March 1865 Hongkong and Shanghai Bank opened to finance growing trade between China, India, Britain's wider empire and Europe. Britain had made Hong Kong its crown colony after the First Opium War, and merchants there wanted their own bank. It soon issued locally denominated banknotes in both cities, was incorporated by Hong Kong ordinance in 1866 as The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, and opened in Yokohama that year.

Britannica, "HSBC Holdings PLC"
sources.confirms: The article says HSBC originated as the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation in 1865 and mentions offices in Hong Kong.
sources.qualifies: It gives no month or day for the opening in Hong Kong.

hsbc-founded-1865.detail: Founder Thomas Sutherland of shipping line P&O wanted it run on "sound Scottish banking principles". Its shares were among 13 securities first traded on Shanghai's stock exchange.

international-telegraph-union-1865.summary: In 1865 twenty states founded the International Telegraph Union so telegrams could cross borders. France had hosted them at the first International Telegraph Conference since 1 March; their convention set basic principles for international telegraphy. It adopted Morse code as international telegraph alphabet, protected secrecy of correspondence and gave everyone a right to use international telegraphy. This Union was history's first international standards organisation and survives as today's International Telecommunication Union, oldest of UN agencies.

sources.author: Siefert, Marsha

international-telegraph-union-1865.detail: Between 1849 and 1865 Western European states had tried to standardise communications through bilateral and regional agreements. By 1865 they agreed a comprehensive framework was needed to standardise equipment, set uniform operating instructions and lay down common tariff and accounting rules.

jiangnan-arsenal-1865.summary: In 1865 Qing officials opened Jiangnan Arsenal in Shanghai to make rifles and warships. Zeng Guofan, Viceroy of Liangjiang, oversaw its plans; Li Hongzhang carried out its establishment. It became the largest Self-Strengthening arsenal, with an annual budget above 400,000 silver taels from 1869, and East Asia's largest weapons factory in the Tongzhi era. It built China's first domestically produced steamboat, Huiji, in 1868, made China's first domestic steel in 1891, and ran its own language school, translation house and technical school.

Britannica, "Li Hongzhang"
sources.confirms: The article says Li Hongzhang maintained an interest in Western-style arsenals he had established in Nanjing and Shanghai.
sources.qualifies: The article does not name the Jiangnan Arsenal or give its establishment date.

sources.author: Meng, Yue
sources.venue: East Asian Science Technology and Medicine

jiangnan-arsenal-1865.verification_note: The Britannica article supports Li Hongzhang's involvement with a Shanghai arsenal but does not identify it as the Jiangnan Arsenal or date its establishment. A Tier 1 journal article is confirmed bibliographically only, with no text read.
jiangnan-arsenal-1865.detail: Its shipyard, plant and machinery were first leased from Thomas Hunt and Company, an American firm in Shanghai's foreign concessions. Concession authorities balked at arms manufacture on their territory, so Chinese authorities bought that plant and combined it with old Suzhou and Anqing arsenal assets and new equipment Yung Wing purchased in America. Most senior technical staff were Westerners.

lister-antiseptic-1865.summary: From 1865 Lister used carbolic acid to kill germs in surgery, and patients stopped dying of infected wounds. He introduced it at Glasgow Royal Infirmary to sterilise instruments, skin, sutures, hands and wards. Walking home with Glasgow chemistry professor Thomas Anderson, Lister had heard of Louis Pasteur's research showing that living organisms caused fermentation and putrefaction; he read Pasteur's papers and concluded that germs, not air, caused putrefaction in wounds. He published his results in The Lancet in five instalments from 10 March 1867.

Britannica, "Joseph Lister | Biography, Facts, & Antiseptic Medicine"
sources.confirms: The article says Lister began antisepsis experiments in Glasgow, became acquainted with Pasteur's work in 1865, first successfully used his method on August 12, 1865, and published cases in March 1867.

sources.title: Lister, Joseph Jackson, "On a New Method of Treating Compound Fracture, Abscess, Etc.," The Lancet 89 (1867)
sources.author: Lister, Joseph Jackson
sources.confirms: Bibliographic record confirms a Lancet article titled "On a New Method of Treating Compound Fracture, Abscess, Etc." dated 1867; text not read.

This evidence does not establish his full set of antiseptic practices or the claim that patients stopped dying. Its Tier 1 source was confirmed only bibliographically.
lister-antiseptic-1865.detail: Most doctors then blamed wound infection on miasma, chemical damage from "bad air", and wards had no facilities for washing hands or wounds. Hearing that creosote had treated sewage in Carlisle, he obtained carbolic acid from Anderson. On 12 August 1865 he first succeeded, dressing with carbolic-soaked lint and putty 11-year-old James Greenlees's compound fracture, whose leg a cart wheel had crushed; after slightly over six weeks his bones had fused without suppuration.

picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0, via Wellcome Collection

locomotive-act-red-flag-1865.summary: In 1865 Britain made road steam engines crawl behind a man on foot, a law aimed at heavy agricultural traction engines, though it is often blamed for holding back Britain's motor car for 30 years. It limited road locomotives to 2 mph in towns and 4 mph in open country and required three crew, one of whom, in practice usually a boy, walked 60 yards ahead carrying a red flag. Its Locomotives on Highways Act 1896 freed light vehicles under 3 tons from all these rules and set 14 mph, which let Britain's motor industry develop.

locomotive-act-red-flag-1865.detail: Road locomotives then meant steam traction and agricultural engines. By 1860 these had prominent chimneys, burned coal, blasted steam unmuffled and ran up to 8 feet wide, as broad as narrow lanes. An 1861 act had already limited their size and weight and set 5 mph in towns and 10 mph outside. In 1878 Parliament dropped that flag but kept a man walking twenty yards ahead to help approaching horses and carriages, with speed limits unchanged.

picture.credit: author unknown, scan by Havang(nl), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

london-sewers-bazalgette-1865.summary: In 1865 Bazalgette's 82 miles of intercepting sewers opened in London, carrying waste out of London and ending its cholera epidemics. Bazalgette's main sewers intercepted outflows that had run freely through London's streets to the Thames and carried them east to pumping stations at Deptford, Crossness, Abbey Mills and Chelsea, which released sewage into the river at high tide. Its premise was wrong, but by removing causal bacteria from water supplies they mostly eliminated cholera where they served and reduced typhus and typhoid.

london-sewers-bazalgette-1865.detail: Parliament had passed an enabling act in 1858 in response to that summer's Great Stink. Cholera had killed 14,137 Londoners in 1849 and 10,738 in 1853; medical opinion blamed foul air, miasma, and expected enclosed sewers to remove it, while John Snow's correct view that contaminated water spread cholera was not yet accepted. Albert Edward, Prince of Wales, opened it in 1865, though completion took ten more years. Bazalgette checked every connection himself; Queen Victoria knighted him in 1875.

maxwell-equations-1865.summary: In 1865 James Clerk Maxwell united electricity, magnetism and light in one set of equations; every radio signal follows from them. Physicist Freeman Dyson called this paper "the most important event of the nineteenth century in the history of the physical sciences". Treating electric and magnetic effects as a single field, Maxwell derived an electromagnetic wave equation whose velocity agreed closely with measured light speeds, and deduced that light is an electromagnetic wave. Part III set out twenty equations known as Maxwell's equations until that name passed to four vector equations selected in 1884; Oliver Heaviside wrote those four in modern vector notation.

maxwell-equations-1865.detail: Maxwell sent it to the Royal Society on 27 October 1864. Members heard it read on 8 December, reviewed by William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, and approved for Philosophical Transactions on 15 June 1865. Albert Einstein took Maxwell's equations as his starting point for special relativity in 1905.

allbutt-clinical-thermometer-1866.summary: Hospital thermometers in the 1860s were a foot long and had to be held in an armpit for twenty minutes while a doctor read its column in place. Thomas Clifford Allbutt, a physician at Leeds General Infirmary, designed in 1866 a self-registering instrument about six inches (15 cm) long whose mercury column stayed at its peak after removal, giving a reading in about five minutes. Harvey and Reynolds of Leeds began making it in 1867, and Allbutt placed no patent on it. Carl Wunderlich's 1868 treatise, drawn from a million readings on 25,000 patients at Leipzig, had just given fever charting its rules; Allbutt's instrument made that routine practical at bedside and in the pocket, and it remained standard until electronic thermometers replaced it a century later.

fuzhou-arsenal-1867.summary: In 1867 Qing officials began a shipyard and naval school at Fuzhou with French engineers; China built steam warships and trained its own officers. Built under orders from Zuo Zongtang and Li Hongzhang, it was one of several Self-Strengthening Movement shipyards and flagship of French assistance to China. French naval officers Prosper Giquel and Paul d'Aiguebelle, on leave from their navy, were contracted to recruit about forty European engineers and mechanics and, within five years, to build forge and Western-style dockyard, eleven transports and five gunboats, and schools of navigation and marine engineering.

sources.confirms: The page states that Zuo built his own arsenal, but does not identify it as the Foochow Navy Yard or date its construction.

Britannica's page mentions Zuo's arsenal without identifying it as Foochow. Its Tier 1 source was assessed via its abstract in the bibliographic record.
fuzhou-arsenal-1867.detail: Planning for it and for Fuzhou Naval College had started in 1866. China supplied materials and labour, 1,600 workers rising past 2,000 by 1872, at an estimated 3 million taels of silver over five years, with ship upkeep partly funded by opium import duties. Its first ship, 150-horsepower Qing Forever, was launched in June 1869. French forces severely damaged it at the Battle of Fuzhou in 1884.

marx-capital-machinery-1867.summary: In 1867 Marx published Capital, arguing that machinery under capitalism lengthens and intensifies work rather than freeing workers. Its central argument is that capitalism's motive force lies in exploiting labour, whose unpaid work is the ultimate source of surplus value and profit: workers sell their capacity to labour as a commodity, but what that labour creates exceeds their wage, and employers keep the difference.

sources.title: Das Kapital - Wikipedia
Britannica, "Das Kapital"
sources.confirms: Britannica says the first volume was published in Berlin in 1867.

sources.title: Marx, Karl, Das Kapital: Kritik der politischen Oekonomie, Vol. 1, Book I, Der Produktionsprocess des Kapitals (1867)
sources.author: Marx, Karl
sources.confirms: The archive catalogue lists the first volume with an 1867 date; the bibliographic record was consulted, not the text.

marx-capital-machinery-1867.detail: Friedrich Engels completed the other volumes from Marx's manuscripts in 1885 and 1894. That process drives capital accumulation, which in turn fosters technological change, creates what Marx called a reserve army of unemployed labour, and tends to push profit rates down, leading to crises and sharper class conflict. On machinery, Marx argued that it transforms production's technical basis, passes workers' skill to machines and leaves each worker "a mere appendage", cheapens commodities and so labour, and arms capital to prolong working days and suppress resistance; workers, he noted, eventually learn to distinguish machinery from its capitalist use.

nobel-dynamite-1866.summary: In 1867 Alfred Nobel patented dynamite in Britain, with an American patent in 1868; Britannica dates its invention to 1867. Nitroglycerin, first made by Ascanio Sobrero in 1847, was far stronger than black powder but so unstable that in 1864 Nobel's own factory blew up, killing his younger brother Emil and others. His 1865 blasting cap, mercury fulminate in a small metal cap fired by shock or moderate heat, let it be set off reliably. Nobel then found kieselguhr, porous siliceous earth, absorbed nitroglycerin to dryness, giving a mixture far safer to handle and ship, and named it dynamite, from Greek dynamis, power. It made mines, tunnels and canals cheap to blast and replaced powder; Nobel enforced his patents tightly.

sources.confirms: The article says Nobel discovered that kieselguhr absorbed nitroglycerin, making the mixture safer to use and easier to handle.
sources.qualifies: The page dates dynamite to 1867, rather than the record's 1866 date.

nobel-dynamite-1866.verification_note: Corrected in November 2026: year moved from 1866 to 1867, its British patent year and Britannica's date for dynamite; his blasting cap now reads 1865 after Britannica.
nobel-dynamite-1866.detail: He moved his work to Germany after his 1864 disaster and sought absorbents that would tame nitroglycerin without weakening it; cement, coal and sawdust failed before diatomaceous earth, fossilised algae dug near his Hamburg factory, succeeded. His US patent 78,317 of 1868 describes nitroglycerin mixed with an absorbent.

picture.credit: Tekniska museet, Public domain, via Europeana

meiji-restoration-industrialization-1868.summary: In January 1868 Emperor Meiji took power back from the shogunate and Japan industrialised in a generation, first non-Western nation to do so. Its government built plants, then sold them to well-connected entrepreneurs, and standardised raw silk exports overtook China's and paid for industrial equipment. Feudalism ended, though these changes provoked Saga and Satsuma rebellions.

sources.title: Aftermath

Its Tier 1 journal source is confirmed bibliographically only; its text was not read.
meiji-restoration-industrialization-1868.detail: The Tokugawa shogunate faced economic and political difficulties, compounded by foreign encroachment. Commodore Perry's expedition had forced Japan open under unequal treaties, putting its ability to defend Japanese sovereignty in question, and Satsuma and Chōshū led an anti-Tokugawa alliance that overthrew it. Meiji's new government moved former lords to Tokyo, reorganised 302 domains into 72 prefectures in 1872 and introduced conscription in 1873. A national railway system and modern communications grew alongside, with coal demand rising for steamships and railroads.

picture.credit: Le Monde Illustre after Alfred Roussin, Bibliotheque nationale de France, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

typewriter-sholes-1868.summary: In 1868 Sholes patented his typewriter, and with it the QWERTY keyboard still under every hand. Sholes and Soule, Wisconsin printers, had built a page-numbering machine in Charles Kleinsteuber's Milwaukee machine shop; Glidden suggested it might print letters too, and in July 1867 showed Sholes a Scientific American article on John Pratt's writing machine, which Sholes thought he could better. It went on sale on 1 July 1874, printing capitals only; Mark Twain was an early buyer.

sources.confirms: The article dates the typewriter patent to June 23, 1868, and says Sholes sold his patent rights in 1873.

typewriter-sholes-1868.detail: Several dozen printing-device patents had already failed as products. James Densmore bought a quarter interest for $600 sight unseen, then provided money and drive through years of refinement. Its typebars hung in a ring and swung up to strike, so adjoining keys pressed in succession could jam; keys were reordered by letter frequency and trial, and after E. Remington and Sons, an arms maker seeking to diversify, contracted to manufacture it in early 1873, Remington swapped its period and R keys so salesmen could type TYPEWRITER on a single row, giving essentially today's QWERTY layout.

ceylon-coffee-rust-tea-1869.summary: In 1869 fungus Hemileia vastatrix appeared on coffee bushes in Ceylon's central highlands. Within fifteen years it cut yields so far that most of 160,000 hectares of coffee were abandoned. Planters replanted with tea using Assam seed; James Taylor's Loolecondera estate had shown tea could be processed on site from 1867. Tamil labour recruited from south India, roads and a railway built for coffee carried new crop, and Colombo became a tea port. This was first global epidemic of a plantation crop disease. Rust then spread through Asia and Africa, reaching Brazil in 1970, and shaped research on fungal pathogens and resistant varieties.

picture.credit: Smartse

jevons-logic-piano-1869.summary: Around 1869 economist William Stanley Jevons had a machine built that solved logic problems at a key press, a step from calculating to reasoning. It was sometimes called the Logic Piano because it resembled an upright piano. In Pure Logic (1864) Jevons had reworked George Boole's system of logic, freeing it from what he considered false mathematical dress, around a single principle, that whatever is true of something is true of its like. He exhibited it before the Royal Society in 1870.

mendeleev-periodic-table-1869.summary: On 6 March 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev's periodic law was announced before Russia's Chemical Society: elements arranged by atomic weight show clear periodicity of properties. He had found this pattern while writing Osnovy khimii (Principles of Chemistry, 1868 to 1871), his course textbook. His 1871 table left gaps where unknown elements should fall, predicted properties of three, and proposed changes to accepted atomic weights. Chemists showed little interest at first; discovery of gallium in 1875, scandium in 1879 and germanium in 1886, matching his predictions, won his system wide acceptance.

John Newlands had noted periodicity by atomic weight in his Law of Octaves of 1864, and Lothar Meyer had classified 28 elements by valence without predicting new ones. Michael Gordin treats date and priority as unsettled, since Mendeleev's system can be dated 1869 or 1871 and Meyer published versions from 1864 to 1870; Eric Scerri calls Mendeleev its leading discoverer because he alone elaborated and defended it for life.

suez-canal-1869.summary: In 1869 the Suez Canal opened, cutting thousands of kilometres between Europe and Asia. French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps had obtained concessions from Sa'id Pasha, Khedive of Egypt and Sudan, in 1854 and 1856 to form his company and build it open to ships of all nations. Running 193 kilometres from Port Said to Suez, it gives ships direct passage between North Atlantic and Indian Ocean through Mediterranean and Red Sea, cutting voyages from Arabian Sea to London by about 8,900 kilometres.

suez-canal-1869.detail: Britain, which controlled its own Cape route to India, opposed it. Shares sold poorly abroad until Cattaui bankers and James de Rothschild promoted them in France, where every French share sold quickly. Some sources estimate that over 1.5 million people from many countries worked on it, more than 30,000 at any time, and that tens of thousands died, many from cholera; after British protests Egypt's viceroy condemned forced corvée labour, halting work for a time.

transcontinental-railroad-1869.summary: On 10 May 1869 America's coasts were joined by rail; crossing it fell to a week. This 1,911-mile line, known then as the Pacific Railroad, joined America's eastern rail network at Council Bluffs, Iowa, to San Francisco Bay; Central Pacific built 690 miles east from Sacramento and Union Pacific 1,085 miles west from Omaha.

transcontinental-railroad-1869.detail: At Promontory Summit, Utah Territory, Central Pacific president Leland Stanford ceremonially tapped a gold "Last Spike", later often called the "Golden Spike", with his silver hammer. Engineer Theodore Judah had lobbied for years and surveyed its route through the Sierra Nevada, its chief obstacle; President Lincoln signed the Pacific Railroad Act on July 1, 1862, financing construction with government and company bonds over public land grants. Central Pacific, short of workers, hired Chinese emigrants, many fleeing clan wars in Guangdong, who did most of its heavy manual labour.

elementary-education-act-1870.summary: On 9 August 1870 W. E. Forster's Elementary Education Act became law, setting up locally elected school boards, funded from rates, to build and manage schools wherever voluntary schools fell short in England and Wales; mass schooling became state business. Census returns of 1861 had shown that of 4.3 million children of primary-school age, 2 million had no schooling at all. Religious teaching in board schools was to be non-denominational. Attendance did not yet become compulsory everywhere: an act of 1880 required it between ages five and ten, fees remained payable until 1891, and leaving age rose to 11 in 1893 and 12 in 1899 (UK Parliament). W. P. McCann (Journal of Educational Administration and History, 1969) surveys voluntary schooling's patchwork on the eve of Forster's act.

elementary-education-act-1870.detail: Pressure came from needing to educate citizens newly enfranchised by Reform Act 1867, and industrialists feared Britain's competitive position suffered for want of effective schooling. Nonconformists objected to Anglican teaching, so its Cowper-Temple clause made religious instruction in board schools non-denominational, and parents could withdraw children from it. Boards could make attendance compulsory by bylaw, covering 40 percent of population by 1873, and pay poor children's fees; between 1870 and 1880 they started or took over 3,000 to 4,000 schools.

indo-european-telegraph-1870.summary: In April 1870 a Siemens line through Russia and Persia linked London to Calcutta by telegraph; a message took 28 minutes instead of weeks. Existing connections were slow and fault-prone: a telegram from London to Karachi averaged 4 days and 9 hours, and the first message on this new route, on 31 January 1870, took 6 days, 8 hours and 44 minutes. At the dress rehearsal on 12 April a telegram crossed from London to Calcutta in 28 minutes, and London to Tehran in one. The line ran until 1931, apart from wartime shutdowns.

indo-european-telegraph-1870.detail: Werner von Siemens had offered to cure this with a continuous line, technically uniform and under a single administration. After long negotiations Siemens & Halske won concessions through Russia in 1867 and Persia in 1868, and the Indo-European Telegraph Company built 4,700 kilometres from Thorn through Warsaw, Odessa, Tiflis and Tehran, with Siemens Brothers in London laying its Black Sea cable.

peruvian-central-railway-1870.summary: In 1870 Peru began a railway from Lima into the Andes that climbed to 4,800 metres; it remained Earth's highest for a century, until Tibet's Qingzang railway opened. Its climb took many switchbacks, around 69 tunnels and 58 bridges; its Galera summit tunnel lies at 4,783 metres. It opened to Chicla by 1878, reached La Oroya in 1893 and Huancayo, 346 kilometres from Callao, in 1908.

peruvian-central-railway-1870.detail: Polish engineers Ernest Malinowski and Edward Jan Habich directed construction. American contractor Henry Meiggs, who had built railways in Chile, had proposed a line from Lima to Jauja in 1868, reportedly telling Peru's government, "I will place rails there, where the llamas walk." His contract, signed on 23 December 1869, set six years for completion and financing by bonds paying 6 percent, on a budget that had climbed to 27 million pounds. Its traffic is mainly minerals from La Oroya, plus fuels, cement and food.

second-industrial-revolution-era-1870.summary: From about 1870 to 1914 steel, oil, electricity and production lines remade work and cut prices of almost everything. Its features were railroad build-out, large-scale iron and steel production using Bessemer converters and open hearth furnaces, widespread machinery and steam power in manufacturing, telegraphy, petroleum, and early electrification and production lines. Productivity gains lowered prices of almost all goods and raised living standards, but also displaced labourers with machines and left factories and ships obsolete within years.

second-industrial-revolution-era-1870.detail: Britain's First Industrial Revolution, which flourished in the later 18th century, had been driven by limited use of steam engines, interchangeable parts and mass production, and was largely water-powered. A slowdown in important inventions preceded 1870. Industrial development then ran fastest in Britain, Germany and the United States, with France, Japan and the Low Countries following. Expanding rail and telegraph lines after 1870 allowed unprecedented movement of people and ideas, feeding new colonialism and globalization. It ended as World War I began.

standard-oil-incorporated-1870.summary: In 1870 Rockefeller founded Standard Oil, soon controlling 90 percent of US refining: modern monopoly was born. Standard grew by sales and acquisitions, shutting down refineries it judged inefficient, and by secret transport deals with railroads; its kerosene price fell from 58 to 26 cents between 1865 and 1870. In 1904 Standard controlled 91 percent of U.S. oil refining and 85 percent of final sales.

sources.qualifies: It dates the 90 to 95 percent refining share to 1880, rather than specifying that Standard reached 90 percent soon after 1870, and it does not say Rockefeller personally incorporated the company.

standard-oil-incorporated-1870.detail: He chose its name to signal reliable standards of quality and service for a young oil industry. In 1872 Rockefeller joined the South Improvement Company, which would have given him shipping rebates and drawbacks on his competitors' oil. On 2 January 1882, 41 investors pooled securities of 40 companies into the Standard Oil Trust under nine trustees. Prompted partly by Ida Tarbell's reporting, the Supreme Court in 1911 found Jersey Standard, by then its holding company, guilty of anticompetitive practices and ordered its breakup into 39 companies, among them forerunners of ExxonMobil and Chevron.

tata-and-sons-1870.summary: In 1870 Jamsetji Tata founded a trading firm with 21,000 rupees; his family went on to build India's steel, power and hotels. Throughout his career he pursued four aspirations: iron and steel making, a landmark hotel, a world-class educational institution and hydroelectric power. In 1903 his company opened the Taj Mahal Hotel on Colaba waterfront, British India's first hotel with electricity; after his death in 1904 his son Dorabji founded Tata Iron and Steel Company in 1907, and western India's first hydro plant became Tata Power.

tata-and-sons-1870.detail: Tata Group, now India's largest conglomerate, dates its establishment to 1868, when his family's fortunes improved substantially through a profitable contract supplying Napier's expedition to Abyssinia. During Bombay's cotton boom of American Civil War years, Jamsetji and his father had been involved with Asiatic Banking Corporation. He bought a bankrupt oil mill at Chinchpokli, converted it to cotton and sold it at a profit after two years, then set up Empress Mill at Nagpur in 1874.

iwakura-mission-1871.summary: From 1871 to 1873 half of Japan's government toured America and Europe to study their factories, schools and armies, then copied them. Japan's new Meiji government sent it with three aims: recognition for Japan's restored imperial dynasty, preliminary renegotiation of the unequal treaties that Western powers had imposed, and that comprehensive study. Treaty renegotiation failed, prolonging the journey by almost four months and pressing its study goal on members. Members returned favorably impressed by Western industrial modernization and with strong impetus to lead similar initiatives at home.

iwakura-mission-1871.detail: Ambassador Iwakura Tomomi led it, with four vice-ambassadors including ministers Ōkubo Toshimichi, Kido Takayoshi and Itō Hirobumi. Its leaders, officials and students sailed from Yokohama on 23 December 1871 aboard SS America for San Francisco. Several students stayed abroad, among them 6-year-old Tsuda Umeko, who later founded Tsuda University. Kume Kunitake's five-volume log, published in 1878, recorded their observations.

kimberley-diamond-fields-1871.summary: In 1871 diamonds were found in weathered kimberlite on Colesberg Kopje, on Vooruitzigt, a farm bought by brothers De Beer, following alluvial finds along Vaal and Orange rivers since 1867. Within two years some 50,000 diggers were working about 1,600 claims of ten metres square, hauling blue ground up a web of ropes and pulleys from a pit later called Big Hole. William Worger shows how African migrant workers, mine owners and Cape Colony officials built a compound system that confined labour and policed diamond theft, while claim consolidation under Cecil Rhodes produced De Beers Consolidated Mines by 1888.

Macfarlane's 2019 survey in Journal of the Southern African Institute of Mining and Metallurgy recounts Erasmus Jacobs's Eureka diamond of 1867 and 1871 discoveries on Vooruitzigt; sources differ on whether Eureka came from near Hopetown or Colesberg Kopje. australian-overland-telegraph-1872.summary: In 1872 a telegraph line crossed Australia from Adelaide to Darwin, cutting news from Britain from months to hours. Charles Todd, South Australia's Superintendent of Telegraphs, headed the project and sent its first message. In 1870 South Australia agreed to build its line within two years for no more than £128,000, while the British-Australian Telegraph Company promised an undersea cable from Banyuwangi, Java, to Darwin. Once linked to the Java cable several months later, communication with Europe fell from months to hours.

australian-overland-telegraph-1872.detail: From 1855 colonists had debated how to reach the new telegraph cable in Java and so Europe. John McDouall Stuart crossed the continent on his sixth attempt in 1862, noting river crossings, timber for poles and water along his route. More than 30,000 wrought iron poles were ordered from England and set 80 metres apart, with repeater stations, including Charlotte Waters and Alice Springs, no more than 250 kilometres apart where water was available year-round.

erewhon-1872.summary: In 1872 Samuel Butler's Erewhon imagined a country that banned machines for fear they would evolve and supplant their makers. Erewhon, an anagram of nowhere, satirises Victorian society in an invented country drawn from Butler's four years sheep farming in New Zealand, where illness is crime and crime is illness.

Reviewers read them as reducing Darwin's theory to absurdity; in his second-edition preface Butler replied that "nothing could be further from my intention". Alan Turing cited Erewhon in "Intelligent Machinery, A Heretical Theory", and Frank Herbert's Dune named its crusade against thinking machines Butlerian Jihad.

first-railway-japan-1872.summary: In 1872 Japan's first railway opened between Tokyo and Yokohama, four years into a modernisation that would make it an industrial power. It is among Japan's oldest stations; only Shinagawa, a few kilometres down that line, is older. Its original station, Shimbashi Teishajō, opened with that line on 14 October 1872, after provisional service from Shinagawa since June, some way east of today's Shimbashi Station. Today's structure opened on 16 December 1909 as Karasumori Station on Tokyo's Yamanote Line. When Tōkaidō Main Line trains were rerouted to Tokyo Station in 1914, Shimbashi Teishajō was demolished for Shiodome freight yard, and Karasumori took its name.

shenbao-newspaper-1872.summary: In 1872 an English merchant founded Shen Bao in Shanghai; it became China's leading newspaper for 77 years. Initial circulation was around 600 copies, printed on a hand-operated Harrild & Sons cylinder press at about 100 pages an hour. Shen Bao quickly became Shanghai's most popular Chinese-language newspaper, faced little competition until the 1890s, and ran until 1949, when Chinese Communist Party authorities discontinued it after taking Shanghai.

tomioka-silk-mill-1872.summary: In 1872 Japan's government opened Tomioka silk mill with French machines; Meiji leaders needed export products, and raw silk and cocoons had made up 86 percent of Japan's exports in 1862. That year silkworm disease in France and Italy and the Taiping Rebellion in China left Japanese silk in high demand, but overproduction and European recovery then cut prices, so the government turned to higher-value silk thread.

tomioka-silk-mill-1872.detail: In 1870 Ōkuma Shigenobu, Itō Hirobumi and Shibusawa Eiichi engaged French engineer Paul Brunat, a raw-silk inspector in Yokohama. He was to build a much larger mill than that year's Italian-equipped Maebashi mill. Brunat bought equipment in France, ordering reeling machines sized for Japanese women, and a brick kiln had to be built in Gunma because brick was not yet in common use. Its 300 French reeling machines made it among the world's largest mills; about 210 women ran half of them at first, and turnover was high. Mitsui & Co. bought it in 1893.

coinage-act-1873.summary: In 1873 the United States stopped coining silver dollars and went onto gold alone; farmers called it the Crime of 1873 for a generation. It took effect April 1 and created a gold standard by default. Since 1792 the United States had been bimetallic: anyone could bring gold or silver to its Mint and receive coins, so a dollar equalled both a legally defined weight of silver and one of gold. Critics denounced this "Crime of '73", and conflict between deflationary gold and inflationary free silver lasted out that century.

coinage-act-1873.detail: Treasury Secretary George Boutwell had Deputy Comptroller John Jay Knox draft a revised Mint law, which Ohio Senator John Sherman introduced. Silver's market price then exceeded its Mint value, so few sought silver dollars and bimetallism's end was rarely mentioned in debate, though not concealed. Knox forecast correctly that Nevada's Comstock Lode and other rich mines would lower silver's price; in 1876 producers brought bullion to Mint offices and learned it could no longer be coined.

gramme-dynamo-1873.summary: In 1873 Gramme's dynamo, shown in Vienna, generated steady current and by accident ran backwards as a motor: power could be sent and used. There Gramme and Fontaine discovered by accident that their device was reversible: connected to any DC power supply, it would spin. Before Gramme's inventions electric motors reached only low power and served mainly as toys or laboratory curiosities; his machine became the first usefully powerful electric motor to succeed industrially.

sources.confirms: Britannica states that a Gramme dynamo was exhibited at the Vienna exhibition in 1873, where it was demonstrated to be reversible and usable as an electric motor.

sources.confirms: Bibliographic record confirms a Journal of the Franklin Institute article on the Gramme dynamo dated 1878; text not read.

gramme-dynamo-1873.detail: Their business, Société des Machines Magnéto-Électriques Gramme, made Gramme dynamos, Gramme rings and Gramme armatures.
