picture.credit: Arnold Wright, Twentieth Century Impressions of Burma (1910)

esperanto-1887.summary: In 1887 Zamenhof published Esperanto, a language built for everyone's second tongue; it has a few million speakers and no country. He intended Esperanto as universal second language to foster world peace and international understanding, and conceived it as neutral tongue with simple, regular grammar. Esperanto became the most successful constructed international auxiliary language and alone has a sizeable population of native speakers, estimated at 2,000; its speakers are concentrated in Europe, East Asia and South America.

sources.title: Esperanto - Wikipedia
Britannica, "Esperanto | Language, Alphabet, Examples, International, Constructed, & Artificial"
sources.confirms: Britannica states that Zamenhof published the first Esperanto textbook on July 26, 1887.
sources.qualifies: Britannica calls it the first Esperanto textbook, rather than specifically the first book.

sources.title: Zamenhof, Ludwik, Dr. Esperanto's International Language: Introduction and Complete Grammar. Por Angloj
sources.author: Zamenhof, Ludwik
sources.confirms: The archive catalogue dates this work to 1887 and identifies Zamenhof as its creator; catalogue record confirms the publication, text not read.

sources.title: Tonkin, H., "One Hundred Years of Esperanto: A Survey"
sources.author: Tonkin, H.
sources.confirms: The academic index record identifies a survey titled "One Hundred Years of Esperanto"; bibliographic record only, with no abstract text provided.

esperanto-1887.verification_note: Britannica and an 1887 archive catalogue support its publication date, while Britannica describes it as a textbook. That archive record and a journal index entry are bibliographic evidence only; the index entry has no abstract.
esperanto-1887.detail: Zamenhof, Jewish ophthalmologist from Białystok, then in the Russian Empire and now in Poland, wrote under his pseudonym Doktoro Esperanto, meaning one who hopes. He called his creation simply la Lingvo Internacia, international language; early speakers grew fond of his pen name and made it its name. Johann Martin Schleyer's Volapük had shown demand for such languages in the 1880s, and when Volapük's movement collapsed, many Volapük clubs became Esperanto clubs.

picture.alt: Cover of French edition of Zamenhof's Unua Libro, first Esperanto textbook, published in Warsaw in 1887.
picture.credit: L. L. Zamenhof, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

hertz-radio-waves-1887.summary: In 1887 Heinrich Hertz made and detected radio waves in his laboratory, making radio and television possible. He built a radiator of two collinear one-metre wires with a spark gap between their inner ends and zinc spheres on their outer ends, and received the waves with a resonant loop antenna with its own micrometer spark gap, where sparks showed detection. Hertz saw no practical use; within six years Guglielmo Marconi began developing wireless telegraphy from his results.

sources.title: Heinrich Hertz
Britannica, "Heinrich Hertz | Radio Waves, Electromagnetic Theory, Electrodynamics"
sources.confirms: Britannica states that Hertz produced electromagnetic waves in the laboratory and measured their length and velocity.
sources.qualifies: Britannica places this laboratory work between 1885 and 1889, without specifying 1887 or stating that he detected the waves.

sources.title: Hertz, H., "Ueber sehr schnelle electrische Schwingungen," Annalen der Physik 267 (1887)
sources.author: Hertz, H.
sources.confirms: Bibliographic record confirms an 1887 publication by H. Hertz titled "Ueber sehr schnelle electrische Schwingungen"; text not read.

hertz-radio-waves-1887.verification_note: Hertz's first experiment was Nov 1886; papers to the Berlin Academy began Nov 1887 and free-space waves were shown in 1888. 1887 is a conventional midpoint; mark approximate or note. || Britannica confirms Hertz's laboratory production of electromagnetic waves during 1885-1889, but does not specify detection or 1887. The 1887 primary publication is confirmed bibliographically only, so the sources do not establish the full event and date claim.
hertz-radio-waves-1887.detail: Maxwell had held that light consisted of electromagnetic waves of short wavelength, but no one had proved this or generated waves of other wavelengths. Hertz's teacher Hermann von Helmholtz had suggested testing Maxwell's theory as his doctoral subject in 1879, and Hertz had judged it too difficult. In autumn 1886, newly professor at Karlsruhe, he noticed that discharging a Leyden jar into a coil produced sparks in another. Beginning in November 1887, he sent papers to Helmholtz at Berlin Academy, including papers in 1888 that showed transverse waves travelling through free space at finite speed.

picture.alt: Portrait photograph of Heinrich Hertz, from Tekniska museet's collection.
picture.credit: Tekniska museet, Public domain, via Europeana

korean-gyeongbokgung-electric-light-1887.summary: In 1887 Korea's first electric light came on in King Gojong's palace in Seoul, run by an Edison plant. Gojong, who saw electricity as a symbol of national enlightenment and self-strengthening, had sent envoys to the United States in 1883 that toured modern facilities, and on September 4, 1884 his government ordered an electric light plant from Edison Electric Light Company. Steam from its coal-fired boiler drove an engine belted to two 3 kW Edison dynamos. Experience gained lighting royal palaces led Gojong to establish Seoul Electric Company in 1898.

sources.title: Gyeongbokgung - Wikipedia
Moon-Hyon Nam, "The Early History of Korean Electric Light and Power Development", Transactions of the Royal Asiatic Society Korea Branch, vol. 86 (2011), pp. 41-59
"Site of 1st electricity generation found", The Korea Times, reporting the National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage excavation
sources.author: The Korea Times
sources.confirms: The National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage located the 1887 Jeongideungso power plant site at Gyeongbokgung and states Korea's first electric lamp was lit between January and March 1887 under an 1884 contract with Edison's company, lighting Geoncheonggung and Hyangwonjeong.
sources.qualifies: News report of a government heritage institute's announcement.

korean-gyeongbokgung-electric-light-1887.detail: One coup attempt that December delayed it. Edison recommended engineer William McKay, who reached Seoul in November 1886 and between December and January built a single-storey powerhouse on high ground between Gojong's residence and its lotus pond, which supplied boiler water. First use is not dated with certainty; January 26, 1887 is most probable, only seven years after Edison's bulb and four and a half after Pearl Street station.

picture.alt: Ogawa Kazumasa's 1886 panoramic photograph of Gyeongbokgung palace in Seoul, a year before electric lights were lit there.
picture.credit: Ogawa Kazumasa, Smithsonian National Anthropological Archives, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

macarthur-forrest-cyanide-1887.summary: In 1887 MacArthur and the Forrest brothers patented dissolving gold from ore with cyanide. Gold mining on South Africa's Rand had slowed in the 1880s because new deposits were pyritic ore, from which older chlorination methods recovered little. MacArthur-Forrest process suspended crushed ore in cyanide solution, which leached out gold; dissolved gold was then recovered, at first on zinc. First used there in 1890, it led, despite operational imperfections, to an investment boom as larger mines opened.

sources.title: Gold cyanidation - Wikipedia
Britannica, "Cyanide process | Gold Extraction, Leaching & Recovery"
sources.confirms: The article identifies 1887 as the year John S. MacArthur, Robert W. Forrest, and William Forrest invented the cyanide process for extracting gold and silver.
sources.qualifies: It describes the process as invented in 1887, rather than confirming the record's patent claim, and covers silver as well as gold.

sources.title: Lougheed, Alan L., "The Discovery, Development, and Diffusion of New Technology: The Cyanide Process for the Extraction of Gold, 1887-1914," Prometheus 7 (1989)
sources.author: Lougheed, Alan L.
sources.confirms: Abstract read via index record: the cyanide process improved gold extraction from unoxidised ores and, because of its low cost, enabled treatment of lower-grade ores.

sources.title: Macathure, J. S., "The macarthur-Forrest process of gold extraction," Journal of the Society of Chemical Industry 9 (1890)
sources.author: Macathure, J. S.
sources.venue: Journal of the Society of Chemical Industry
sources.confirms: Bibliographic record confirms a 1890 article titled "The macarthur-Forrest process of gold extraction"; text not read.

macarthur-forrest-cyanide-1887.verification_note: Process developed in Glasgow in 1887 (europe); first used on the Rand in 1890. Either region europe for 1887, or year 1890 with africa. || Britannica confirms its 1887 invention, and Lougheed's journal abstract supports its importance for unoxidised and low-grade ores. Its patent claim and details about first use on the Rand and a resulting investment boom are not established by these records. Its Tier 1 sources were accessed as an abstract via an index record and a bibliographic record, respectively.
macarthur-forrest-cyanide-1887.detail: Several patents were issued that year. Carl Wilhelm Scheele had discovered in 1783 that gold dissolves in watery cyanide solutions, and Bagration, Elsner and Faraday established in the 1840s that each gold atom needs two cyanide ions, forming a soluble gold-cyanide complex. Around 1900 Charles Merrill and Thomas Crowe improved recovery using vacuum and zinc dust. Cyanidation now accounts for about 90 percent of gold production, and remains controversial because cyanide is toxic.

pneumatic-tire-dunlop-1887.summary: In 1887 Dunlop fitted air-filled rubber tyres to his son's tricycle in Belfast; on 18 May 1889 cyclist Willie Hume won all four events at Queen's College Sports in Belfast on them. Using his experience with rubber devices, Dunlop had fitted an inflatable tyre to a wooden disc 96 centimetres across in his yard, rolled it alongside his metal tricycle wheel, and watched that wheel stop while his pneumatic wheel ran on to a gatepost and rebounded. Two years after his patent Dunlop learned it was invalid: Robert William Thomson had patented pneumatic tyres in 1846 and 1847.

sources.title: John Boyd Dunlop - Wikipedia
Britannica, "John Boyd Dunlop"
sources.confirms: Britannica states that Dunlop constructed a pneumatic tire for his son's tricycle in 1887 and patented it the following year.
sources.qualifies: Britannica notes that the principle of the pneumatic tire had already been patented in 1846.

sources.title: "The Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre for Vehicles," The Lancet (1895)
sources.confirms: Bibliographic record confirms a Lancet article titled "The Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre for Vehicles" dated 1895; text not read.

sources.title: "Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Company, Ltd., and Pneumatic Tyre Company, Ltd. v. Excelsior Tyre Cement and Rubber Company and J. F. Barker," Reports of Patent, Design and Trade Mark Cases 18 (1901)
sources.venue: Reports of Patent, Design and Trade Mark Cases
sources.confirms: Bibliographic record confirms a 1901 case report involving the Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Company; text not read.

pneumatic-tire-dunlop-1887.detail: Dunlop, a Scottish veterinary surgeon born on an Ayrshire farm in 1840, had moved to Ireland in 1867 and by the mid 1880s ran one of Ireland's largest veterinary practices. He then put pneumatics on both rear wheels, tested them at Cherryvale sports ground, and was granted his patent on 7 December 1888. Cyclist Willie Hume won all four events at Queen's College Sports in Belfast on 18 May 1889 on Dunlop's tyres, beating sons of Harvey du Cros, president of Irish Cyclists' Association, who then formed a company with Dunlop. Dunlop sold out in 1895.
